'''''Hydrocotyle vulgaris''''', the '''marsh pennywort''', '''common pennywort''', '''water naval''', '''money plant''', '''lucky plant''', '''dollarweed''' or '''copper coin''',<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |accessdate=2014-10-17 }}</ref> is a small creeping [[aquatic plant|aquatic]] [[perennial plant]] native to [[North Africa]], [[Europe]], the [[Caucasus]] and parts of the [[Levant]].<ref>{{cite web | url=https://hgic.clemson.edu/factsheet/dollarweed/ | title=Dollarweed }}</ref>

==Description==
[[File:Gewöhnlicher_Wassernabel_PICT8939.JPG|left|thumb|220px|Shield-shaped leaf]]
The plant has an umbrella-like leaf and lives commonly in wet places such as wetlands, marshes and swamps, sometimes even in deeper water. It grows as a [[perennial plant|perennial]] [[herbaceous plant]] and only reaches stature heights of 5 to 20 centimeters. With a slight smell of carrot, it is edible.{{Cn|date=May 2021}}

This marsh plant forms numerous, up to 1 meter long, creeping [[Offshoot (plant)|offshoot]]s. The serrated, rounded, shield-shaped leaves can have a diameter of up to 4 centimeters, but are often smaller. The approach of the long, hairy [[petiole (botany)|petiole]]s is located in the middle of the leaf underside. The leaves are fresh green, shiny waxy and shows a clear, radially extending vein.{{Cn|date=May 2021}}

The tiny, inconspicuous, [[hermaphrodite]] flowers are in low-flowered doldigen{{?|What is "low flowered doldigen"|date=June 2021}} [[inflorescence]]s or whorls, with the stems of the inflorescence about half as long as those of the leaves. The petals are greenish, white or reddish. The flowering period is from July to August. The fruits are flat, warty and winged.<ref>Siegmund Seybold (ed.): Schmeil-Fitschen interactive . CD-ROM version 1.1. Quelle & Meyer, Wiebelsheim 2002, {{ISBN|3-494-01327-6}} .</ref>

==Cultivation==
A low maintenance plant, it prefers to grow in reliably moist [[humus]] under a full sun or in part shade, [[house plant|indoors]] or outdoors, though it can tolerate full shade as well. It may also be grown as an aquatic plant in mud at the side of a pond or [[water garden]] in up to 2 inches of stagnant water. Despite its habitat in water, over-watering may still cause [[root rot]].<ref>Christel Kasselmann: Aquarienpflanzen. Ulmer Verlag, Stuttgart 1995; 2., überarbeitete und erweiterte Auflage 1999, {{ISBN|3-8001-7454-5}}, S. 306.</ref>

==Population==
The plant is distributed and plentiful throughout much of its range in Europe, North Africa and Western Asia. Nonetheless, it is classed as [[critically endangered]] in Croatia, [[Vulnerable species|vulnerable]] in Switzerland and [[near threatened]] in Norway. Furthermore, the plant is protected under regional legislation in France.<ref name="iucn status 12 November 2021" />

==Ecology==
In Britain it is the only native ''[[Hydrocotyle]]'', growing in wet places such as fens, swamps, bogs and marshes. For example, it is a component of [[purple moor grass and rush pastures]] – a type of [[Biodiversity action plan|Biodiversity Action Plan habitat]]. The flowers rarely bloom; mostly [[self-pollination]] takes place. [[Vegetative propagation]] occurs through foothills. In wild plant gardens, the marsh pennywort is used for the planting of garden ponds, and also as [[aquarium]] plant.<ref>Manfred A. Fischer, Wolfgang Adler, Karl Oswald: Excursion flora for Austria, Liechtenstein and South Tyrol . 2nd, improved and extended edition. Upper Austria, Biology Center of the Upper Austrian Provincial Museums, Linz 2005, {{ISBN|3-85474-140-5}} .</ref>
